rules_text:
Rules summary On your turn: Play cards Claim habitats Draw cards Play Cards - play any number of cards from your hand with the same numeric value - they must be played on a new set or an existing set (of the same animal kind) - the number you play must be equal to or greater than the card on the top of the stack Claim Habitats Count the number of cards on the stack and claim a Habitat Card that is a) of the same animal type and b) equal to or less than the number. The stack must be of the stack that you just played at least one card to. You cannot play Bear Forest cards and then claim a Habitat Card for the Goose Mist on that same turn. Draw Cards Draw cards from the display equal to the numeric value of the cards you played at the beginning of your turn. So if you played three cards with a value 1, you would only draw 1 card from the display. Note that you have a hand limit of 8 cards. End Game When someone has 15 Balance Points, every other player gets a turn and then the game is over. Tiebreakers: highest value Habitat card, and the next, and the next, or share the victory

[Rating: 6/10] At first glance, it seems like a nice and simple set collection game with very clear rules. The longer it goes, the more random it becomes. By the end, players don’t have many choices left, and the game’s pace really slows down.

[Rating: 6/10] This is a perfectly fine game, but it just doesn’t stand out in the crowded field of small box card games. I’ve played it a couple of times, and it’s just a little forgettable. It’s the type of game that if someone asked to play it, I would be happy to play. But I don’t know that I would ever think of it or choose it.

[Rating: 6/10] Perhaps I hyped the game up a bit because of the designer, Hisashi Hayashi. We played once, and I was just getting the worst draws, so I said we had to play again. I played better, but my frustration during the game persisted. Everyone else at the table was enjoying it, so it was clearly just a me issue, and most people will enjoy this. I did enjoy it more than Bohnanza, which I would compare it to.

[Rating: 6/10] Only one play so far, but that left me behind with some frustration. If all the high cards are taken just before me and you are only left with 1's, then you can get really stuck.   Not that a lot of 1's is bad, as often you can then start a big series, but you only get to take 1 card, which means your next turn will probably be horrible.  So it's clear I don't have the hang of it and I'll have to give it an other shot.

[Rating: 6.5/10] Circadia is a stunning card game where players are invoking spirit animals to reset the natural rhythm of the natural world.   In Circadia, players play cards into one of three spirit animal sets. The sets must go in ascending order (à la Lost Cities). Players can play as many cards as they have of one value, and the value played determines the number of cards the player draws. Before the end of their turn, the player can trade in their sets for points in a market. These score cards are either marked as day and night.
